The asynchronous handler wraps anything that is not a coroutine function in `sync_to_async`, so that it runs in a thread, and awaits the result either way (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response`, `django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response_async`).
So `as_view` asks the class, through `View.view_is_async`, and if the answer is yes it marks the function with `inspect.markcoroutinefunction` (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`).

A class with both kinds, like the class *Muddle*, raises `ImproperlyConfigured` whether the property is read or `as_view` asks it, and since `as_view` asks as the URLconf is imported, that is when the error appears, naming the class (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.view_is_async`):

Under an `ASGIHandler`, then, the work a class does before its handler method, in `View.__init__`, `View.setup` and `View.dispatch` and whatever a subclass adds to them, runs on the event loop's thread, so code there that blocks holds up the event loop (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`, `django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response_async`).

Each therefore asks `view_is_async` and, when it is true, returns its response from inside a small coroutine (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.options`, `django/views/generic/base.py:View.http_method_not_allowed`).

Each therefore asks `view_is_async` and, when it is true, returns its response from inside a small coroutine (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.options`, `django/views/generic/base.py:View.http_method_not_allowed`).
None of the handler methods in `django/views/generic/` is written with `async def`, so under an asynchronous handler a generic view runs in a thread, like any other function.

So each decorator written in `django/views/decorators/` defines its wrapper twice, once with `def` and once with `async def`, and picks one as it is applied, by asking `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` of the view.
The wrapper for a coroutine function awaits the view (`django/views/decorators/http.py:require_http_methods`).

The decorators made from a middleware get their two wrappers from `make_middleware_decorator`, written the same way ([A middleware as a decorator](middleware-decorators.md#a-coroutine-view)) (`django/utils/decorators.py:make_middleware_decorator`).
`method_decorator` does the equivalent for a method: when the method it replaces is a coroutine function, it marks the replacement (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).

Support for a coroutine function came in 5.0 to the decorators of `django/views/decorators/` that its release notes list as ones that "now support wrapping asynchronous view functions" (`docs/releases/5.0.txt`).

`method_decorator` began to mark its replacement in 5.2 (`docs/releases/5.2.txt`).

Put to each wrapper, the test finds that those of `django/views/decorators/` keep the `async def` function a coroutine function, and that `non_atomic_requests` does not ([When the test is fooled](#when-the-test-is-fooled)).

`View.dispatch` is written with `def`, so at each request the decorator is handed a partial around the bound `dispatch`, which is not a coroutine function, and its `def` wrapper gets back the coroutine `get` made where it expected a response (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).
The documentation's remedy is an `async def` override of `dispatch` for `method_decorator` to decorate, and the decorator then chooses its `async def` wrapper (`docs/topics/async.txt`).

The asynchronous handler makes the same check, in `check_response`, the method that also refuses a view's `None` ([What the handler asks of a view](callable.md#what-a-view-may-return)), and raises the same error (`django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler.check_response`).

Its wrapper is a plain function (in 5.2, 6.0 and 6.1 the decorator set its mark on the view itself and returned it), so the handler calls it as one and gets back the view's coroutine, not yet started (`django/db/transaction.py:_non_atomic_requests`).
